blocks.text: Design a distributed job scheduler, the system responsible for running jobs, such as a nightly billing run or an hourly data sync, on a defined schedule, reliably and exactly once per trigger, even though the scheduler itself runs as multiple nodes for high availability and can itself experience downtime. This is the second problem in this project's Asynchronous Systems category, and its core difficulty is coordination: many independent scheduler nodes must agree on who executes a given trigger, and the scheduler must have a deliberate, honest answer for what happens to a trigger that was missed entirely while the whole scheduler was unavailable.
blocks.content: Design a distributed job scheduler, the system responsible for running jobs, such as a nightly billing run or an hourly data sync, on a defined schedule, reliably and exactly once per trigger, even though the scheduler itself runs as multiple nodes for high availability and can itself experience downtime. This is the second problem in this project's Asynchronous Systems category, and its core difficulty is coordination: many independent scheduler nodes must agree on who executes a given trigger, and the scheduler must have a deliberate, honest answer for what happens to a trigger that was missed entirely while the whole scheduler was unavailable.

blocks.alt: Multiple scheduler nodes race to claim a due trigger, with exactly one winning and executing it, while a scheduler recovering from downtime applies each job's own catch-up policy to decide what happens to any triggers that were missed

blocks.text: The two techniques that define this design are a distributed lock per job trigger, guaranteeing that even with many scheduler nodes running for availability, exactly one of them executes any single trigger, directly reusing this project's existing locking service design as the underlying mechanism, and a per-job, configurable missed-trigger catch-up policy, since a scheduler that was itself down when a trigger's time passed needs a deliberate, explicit answer, not an accidental one, for whether that missed run should still happen.

blocks.text: A user should be able to define a job with a recurring schedule and a specific action to run. When a job's trigger time becomes due, the system should execute it exactly once, even with multiple scheduler nodes running concurrently. Each job should be configurable with its own missed-trigger catch-up policy: catch up on every missed trigger, catch up on only the single most recent one, or skip missed triggers entirely. The system should record the outcome of every execution attempt. A single job's failure or unusually long runtime should not affect any other job's own schedule.

The system should record the outcome of every execution attempt. A single job's failure or unusually long runtime should not affect any other job's own schedule.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are this design's defining correctness concerns.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are this design's defining correctness concerns.

blocks.alt: A job never executes twice for the same trigger, missed triggers are handled deliberately rather than silently lost, a due job starts within seconds, one job's failure never affects another, and the scheduler itself recovers cleanly from its own downtime

blocks.text: A job never executing twice for the same trigger matters because running the same billing job twice for the same day would be a real, damaging correctness bug, not merely a cosmetic one. Missed triggers being handled deliberately means whichever catch-up policy applies, the decision to run or skip a missed trigger must be an explicit, configured choice, never an accident of how the scheduler happened to recover. A due job starting within seconds matters for time-sensitive jobs like an hourly sync, which should not drift meaningfully behind its intended cadence. One job's failure never affecting another means a single slow or stuck job should never delay or starve every other scheduled job sharing the same infrastructure. And clean recovery from the scheduler's own downtime means the scheduler process itself can restart or fail over at any time and must resume correctly afterward.

blocks.text: This design assumes job execution itself runs inside an already-isolated sandbox, so a job's own code or command cannot affect the scheduler process or any other job's execution, keeping this design's own scope focused on scheduling and coordination rather than sandboxing mechanics. A job whose previous execution is still running when its next trigger becomes due is assumed to have that next trigger simply queued behind it rather than run concurrently or silently dropped, since concurrent runs of the same job are rarely safe and queuing is the simplest broadly correct default. Retry-with-backoff for a failed execution is assumed to be a thin layer on top of the same per-trigger claim-and-execute mechanism described here, reusing it rather than requiring separate coordination logic.

blocks.text: A large platform can realistically have tens of thousands of distinct scheduled jobs active at once, with many of them sharing the exact same trigger time, everything scheduled for midnight being the obvious example. Claiming a due trigger needs to resolve in a small fraction of a second, so that execution genuinely starts promptly rather than being delayed by the coordination step itself.

blocks.text: Multiple scheduler nodes, run for high availability, independently evaluate every job's schedule against the current time. When a trigger becomes due, each node that notices it attempts to claim it through the distributed trigger lock; exactly one wins and hands the execution off to the shared worker pool, which reads and writes the job store for definitions and execution history.

blocks.text: When a specific job's specific trigger time becomes due, every scheduler node that notices it attempts to claim it. The first node to successfully claim it is the only one that executes the job for that trigger; every other node observes it as already claimed and does not execute it again. This directly reuses the same locking mechanics as this project's existing locking service design, applied here per job trigger rather than per arbitrary resource.

blocks.alt: Every scheduler node races to claim a due trigger, the first to succeed executes the job, and every other node sees it already claimed and does not execute it again

blocks.text: When the scheduler recovers after any period of downtime, it compares each job's full schedule against how much real time actually passed. Any trigger time that fell within that downtime window without ever being executed is a missed trigger, detected explicitly rather than silently forgotten.

blocks.alt: On recovery, the scheduler compares each job's full schedule against elapsed downtime, and any trigger time that passed without executing is explicitly identified as missed

blocks.text: Each job carries its own configured policy for what happens to its missed triggers. Catch-up-on-all executes once for every single missed trigger, in order. Coalesce executes exactly once, only for the most recent missed trigger, treating the earlier ones as superseded. Skip executes for none of them at all, simply waiting for the next naturally upcoming trigger.

blocks.text: TriggerClaim is deliberately a small, fast-write table keyed by job and trigger time together, since a claim attempt needs to resolve in a small fraction of a second on the hot coordination path.

blocks.text: A job's schedule and catch-up policy are modeled as small, infrequently-changing configuration, read constantly by every scheduler node's evaluation loop but written only when a user explicitly updates the job. Trigger claims and execution records, by contrast, are write-heavy and append-only, one row added per trigger claimed and per execution attempted, read far more often for later audit and debugging than for any live scheduling decision.

A recovering scheduler compares a job's full schedule against elapsed downtime, identifies its missed triggers, and applies that job's own configured catch-up policy to decide which of them actually execute now

blocks.text: The happy path is the lock race flow above, a due trigger claimed cleanly by exactly one node. The workflow worth walking through separately is recovery after downtime: rather than either blindly re-running every missed trigger for every job, which could badly overload the system after a long outage, or silently dropping all of them, which could hide a real correctness gap for a job that genuinely needed every run, each job's own explicit, pre-configured policy resolves the ambiguity deliberately and predictably.

blocks.alt: A job's schedule definition, read on every evaluation cycle by every scheduler node, is cached until the job definition itself is next updated

blocks.text: Caching job schedule definitions aggressively is essential, since every scheduler node re-evaluates every job's schedule on every cycle, and schedules themselves change far less often than they are read.

blocks.alt: Every trigger that becomes due, across every job, is placed into a shared job execution queue, drained independently by a pool of workers

blocks.text: Separating the scheduling decision, which node claims a trigger, from the execution itself, which worker actually runs it, through a shared queue is what keeps one job's slow or stuck execution from ever blocking the scheduler's own evaluation loop for every other job.
blocks.content: Separating the scheduling decision, which node claims a trigger, from the execution itself, which worker actually runs it, through a shared queue is what keeps one job's slow or stuck execution from ever blocking the scheduler's own evaluation loop for every other job.

blocks.alt: A claimed, due job execution is assigned to whichever worker in the shared pool is currently free

blocks.text: Because claiming a trigger and executing it are deliberately separate steps, the execution worker pool can be load balanced using ordinary, simple least-busy-worker assignment, with no need to route based on which scheduler node happened to win a given trigger's claim.
blocks.content: Because claiming a trigger and executing it are deliberately separate steps, the execution worker pool can be load balanced using ordinary, simple least-busy-worker assignment, with no need to route based on which scheduler node happened to win a given trigger's claim.

blocks.alt: A job execution queue growing faster than the worker pool can drain it triggers adding more workers to the shared pool

blocks.text: Scaling here means growing the shared execution worker pool in response to actual execution load, entirely independent of how many scheduler nodes exist, since scheduler node count is driven by availability needs, not by throughput.

blocks.text: Job definitions scale as a small, read-heavy, easily cached and replicated dataset. Trigger claims and execution history scale as an ordinary, high-write-volume, time-partitioned log, similar in shape to this project's existing time-series design, since both are append-heavy and overwhelmingly queried by a recent time range.

blocks.alt: Which node has claimed one specific trigger is strongly consistent, zero tolerance for a double execution; the historical execution record is only eventually consistent, fine for audit and debugging

blocks.text: The one piece of state this design cannot compromise on is a single trigger's own claim, while the historical execution log lagging slightly is a completely acceptable trade-off, since nothing live depends on reading it instantly.

blocks.alt: One scheduler node failing or restarting mid-operation leaves every other node continuing to evaluate and claim due triggers exactly as before

blocks.text: Running multiple, independent scheduler nodes is itself the primary reliability mechanism, no single node's failure can stop the schedule from running, since the distributed trigger lock ensures whichever nodes remain simply continue claiming and executing due triggers without any special failover logic of their own.

blocks.alt: A scheduled job running inside an isolated execution sandbox cannot affect the scheduler or any other job; without that isolation, a single misbehaving job risks the entire system

blocks.text: Execution sandboxing is this design's defining security concern, distinct from every other category's angle in this project, since a job scheduler by its nature runs arbitrary, user-defined code or commands on a recurring, often unattended basis, making isolation between jobs and the scheduler itself essential.

blocks.text: Trigger claim latency is the most important thing to watch, a rising latency here signals contention or a struggling lock service directly on the path that determines how promptly every job actually starts. The size of a missed-trigger backlog after any scheduler downtime is also worth surfacing prominently, since it directly reflects how much catch-up work, if any, is about to run across the whole platform at once.

blocks.text: A distributed trigger lock paired with a per-job catch-up policy is the right default because it is the only approach that gets both genuine high availability across scheduler nodes and an honest, deliberate answer for what happens to a trigger the scheduler was unable to fire on time.

blocks.text: Separating the lightweight scheduling decision from the potentially heavy execution work is itself a meaningful cost optimization, scheduler nodes stay small and cheap since they only evaluate schedules and claim triggers, while the execution worker pool, the genuinely resource-intensive part, scales independently based on actual job workload rather than scheduler node count. Bounding how many missed triggers a single job's catch-up policy will process at once also prevents an unusually long downtime from triggering a disproportionately expensive recovery burst.

blocks.text: A change to the distributed trigger lock's own claim logic needs the most rigorous possible testing in this system, since any bug there risks either a double execution or a job silently never running at all, both serious correctness failures for jobs like billing runs. Catch-up policy defaults deserve careful, job-by-job review rather than a single platform-wide assumption, since the right answer genuinely differs between a financially critical job and a purely informational one.
